title: Terrible gigs and toughing it out
summary: A barnyard costume gig after the Vanguard, and how the family jobs taught him endurance.

story.theme_name: Band pranks, jokes and gigs gone wrong
story.community_name: Pranks, practical jokes and band humor

blocks.x: But along those lines I’ll try a question that hardly ever works also, and that is, have you ever, do you recall just a terrible gig or series of gigs that you just couldn’t believe you were involved in?

Well there’s, sure. I remember one night I had booked a gig with a group in town, a guy in town here who I’d worked for doing a lot of trade shows. And he said, “You have to go get fitted for a costume.” So I went down to this place where they have theatrical costumes and I went and got fitted for the costume. And he said, “We’re doing this dentists’ convention and the theme is the movie “Tom Jones” so you have to get fitted for the satin pantaloons, the button thing, the George Washington wig, and he said, “I’ll be playing harpsichord and we’ll be playing tunes like “In a Twentieth Century Drawing Room.’” And I was taking anything at that time. This was in the early 70s. Now I had a week at the Village Vanguard. We finished on a Sunday night. The gig was on a Monday. So I finished Jones up on Sunday night, and Monday I go down to this gig at one of the hotels here, and I get on stage and there’s the guys with the harpsichords, they’re all having the George Washington wigs and the guys at the harpsichords was a bass player and a drummer. And we are in straw this thick with goats and chickens and all kinds of livestock with us, and we’re playing, I was playing flute and saxophone. And we’re supposed to be in a barnyard scene. And I thought to myself Jones one night and here the next night.

But you know what? Working with my father as a kid, learning how to work firemen’s picnics and clam bakes and weddings and all of these jobs where you just took them because it was work, I just learned how to tough it out and tough it through. I mean there were times when I played with Elvin that I hated the gig because of certain things going on. Same thing with Buddy. There were nights when you just didn’t do it. But you knew
that it was always going to get better, there was always going to be bad nights and it’s just one of those things. There’s always good nights coming down the road at some point, you hope.
Gee. Well that’s something that students should know about, although those kinds of gigs are hardly around anymore. I think it’s a shame.

I’ve been on bands where I didn’t like all of the players I was playing with. There was one band that I hated everybody in the band except the band boy. I liked the leader. But everybody else I couldn’t stand working with but you had to do it. Once you got on the bandstand you had to function if you want to play. If you don’t want to play the music you walked out. I’ve only walked off a couple of gigs and it’s just because the leaders were so obnoxious — and after working with Buddy that’s one thing I learned about working with Buddy Rich. After you work with Buddy Rich you never took any crap from anybody because you’ve seen the original act. I would watch these guys and they’d say, “I’m out of here, I don’t need this.” You know. And I walked off jazz gigs when very famous guys who I said I saw the original. I don’t need to see a carbon copy, I’m gone. I don’t need the money. At that point I didn’t.
